column4: The section explicitly gathers its covering, faces, and fire in وَتَغْشَىٰ وُجُوهَهُمُ ٱلنَّارُ: the fire itself covers their faces.
The water offered from the fire is like molten metal and يَشْوِى ٱلْوُجُوهَ, making water scorch faces instead of reviving dry ground.
The section cites the revived earth as proof of resurrection; this ayah states that the One who gives the humbled earth life gives the dead life.
Livestock skins become portable houses and their wool, fur, and hair become furnishings, so the camel viewed in 88:17 supplies the earthly room mirrored by the furnished garden.
Milk brought from an animal's belly is سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ, joining camel and drink while reversing the undrinkable draught of 14:17.
The condemned gulps the drink but وَلَا يَكَادُ يُسِيغُهُ; this is the exact swallowing reversal of the easily swallowed milk in 16:66.
فَلْيَنظُرِ ٱلْإِنسَانُ إِلَىٰ طَعَامِهِ repeats the section's summons to look, now directing sight to food rather than the camel.
The command not to enter the Prophet's rooms غَيْرَ نَاظِرِينَ إِنَاهُ brings looking or waiting, food, its moment of ripeness, a room, and the Prophet's proper place into one scene.
وَكُلُّ صَغِيرٍ وَكَبِيرٍ مُّسْتَطَرٌ makes every small and great thing an inscribed line, supplying the record sense the section hears inside مُصَيْطِر.
Their eyes are خَاشِعَةً and abasement covers them because they once declined the call to prostrate; compulsory lowering answers the section's missed voluntary lowering.
A غَاشِيَةٌ مِّنْ عَذَابِ ٱللَّهِ places the section's opening cover beside punishment and asks whether people feel secure from its arrival.
وَلَٰكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ names denial and turning away; 75:31 supplies the refused prayer that makes this the section's bodily reversal.
Immediately after fire covers faces in 14:50, God repays every soul and is سَرِيعُ ٱلْحِسَابِ, joining the section's opening scene to its final accounting.
The next ayah calls the disclosure a proclamation and warning so that people may remember, placing the messenger's reminder after covered faces and divine reckoning in 14:50-51.
Rain gives dead earth life as a sign لِقَوْمٍ يَسْمَعُونَ, joining the life-giving water, earth, and hearing that the section sets against boiling water.
After the face-scorching drink of 18:29, believers recline on adorned couches in gardens with flowing rivers, reproducing the section's two opposed rooms.
فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ contributes the refused prayer; 75:32 then names the denial and turning away cited by the section.
The call to prostrate and their inability to do so begins the scene completed by humbled eyes in 68:43, marking the point when willing bowing is no longer possible.
On that Day voices are خَشَعَتِ ٱلْأَصْوَاتُ and only a whisper is heard, giving the section's covering Day its subdued soundscape.
وَعَنَتِ ٱلْوُجُوهُ makes faces submit before the Living Sustainer, directly joining the face with involuntary lowliness on the Day.
خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ says the Event lowers and raises, gathering the section's lowered and delighted faces, raised heaven and couches, and final reversal of rank.
The Creator of the layered heavens commands the beholder to return sight and ask whether any fissure is visible, closely matching the question that directs sight to creation.
Repeated sight returns خَاسِئًا وَهُوَ حَسِيرٌ, making the very eye that examines the raised heaven come back humbled and exhausted like the section's low, laboring face.
God makes earth فِرَاشًا, heaven بِنَاءً, and rain-produced fruit provision, constructing the world as one furnished room of floor, roof, water, and food.
God raised the heavens without visible pillars and explains the signs so people may be certain of meeting their Lord; the viewed sky proves the awaited meeting.
The One who spread the earth, placed mountains, and made paired fruits follows the raised sky of 13:2, closely paralleling the section's sequence of created objects.
وَٱلسَّمَاءَ رَفَعَهَا places the raised heaven beside the divinely set balance, linking physical elevation to the just measure culminating in حساب.
وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَضَعَهَا لِلْأَنَامِ answers the raised sky of 55:7 with earth laid down, using the room-making motion heard in the section's placed cups and spread floor.
The question whether humans are harder to create or heaven turns looking at the world's construction into an argument for the resurrection scene.
رَفَعَ سَمْكَهَا فَسَوَّاهَا says God raised and proportioned heaven's canopy, a direct parallel to the raised sky in the section.
وَٱلْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ دَحَاهَا follows the raised canopy with earth spread out, reproducing the world's roof-and-floor order.
Water and pasture are brought from the spread earth, showing how its preparation becomes drink and food rather than the sterile provisions of punishment.
The mountains are fixed after heaven and earth, completing the same created landscape shown in 88:18-20.
مَتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ makes that landscape provision for people and livestock, bringing the viewed camel back into the creation sequence.
أَفَلَمْ يَنظُرُوا إِلَى ٱلسَّمَاءِ asks people to look at how heaven was built, adorned, and left without fissures, almost exactly the visual stance of 88:17-18.
The earth is spread and mountains cast into it after the command to inspect heaven, continuing the same downward movement of the gaze.
Blessed water descends from heaven and grows gardens and grain, the life-giving counterpart to the boiling spring of the first half.
Rain is provision for servants, revives a dead land, and is followed by كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ, explicitly turning viewed earth into proof of emergence from graves.
فَٱنظُرْ إِلَىٰٓ ءَاثَارِ رَحْمَتِ ٱللَّهِ commands a look at revived earth and concludes that its Reviver gives the dead life.
Wind, cloud, and rain revive dead land, and كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ explicitly names that scene as the likeness of resurrection.
The long resurrection proof makes lifeless earth stir, swell, and grow after water descends, pairing human recreation with revived ground.
Rain revives dead land and كَذَٰلِكَ نُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ states that bringing forth the dead follows the same visible pattern.
Measured water revives a dead land and كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ turns that earthly change into the reader's own promised emergence.
Creating heaven and earth without weariness establishes God's power to revive the dead, making the viewed construction proof of the Day.
سِيرُوا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَٱنظُرُوا asks people to travel the earth and see how creation began, then states that God produces the final creation.
أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا أَنَّا خَلَقْنَا لَهُم... أَنْعَامًا is the closest general counterpart to looking at how the camel was created.
The created livestock are made tractable, some serving as mounts and some as food, unfolding the fitting of the animal to human life.
Livestock provide benefits and drinks, then the passage asks whether people will give thanks, joining animal, provision, and moral sight.
Livestock are explicitly a lesson: people are given drink from their bellies and receive many benefits and food from them.
Being carried on livestock and ships completes the animal lesson, giving the camel its journeying role beside its drink and materials.
God makes livestock so that some are ridden and some eaten, a direct account of the created fitness contemplated in the camel.
Their benefits, transport of needs, and pairing with ships extend the camel scene into travel and provision.
After those livestock uses God shows His signs and asks which signs people deny, matching the interrogative force of the section's look.
Created livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food, anticipating the skins and fibers made into the earthly room in 16:80.

وَلَكُمْ فِيهَا جَمَالٌ حِينَ تُرِيحُونَ وَحِينَ تَسْرَحُونَ stages the herd's evening return and morning departure, concretizing the day's outward and homeward camel movement heard in the surah's ring.
Livestock carry loads to a land reachable only with hardship, giving the camel-language of advance and return its burdened road.
The companions of the left eat from the tree of Zaqqum, another sterile hell food placed before the camel-like drinking in 56:55.
They drink boiling water after filling their bellies, directly joining hell food and the scalding drink of the section.
فَشَارِبُونَ شُرْبَ ٱلْهِيمِ makes the condemned drink like desperately thirsty camels, bringing camel and hell drink into one explicit image.
Paradise's unspoiled water and milk are set against boiling water that cuts the bowels, expanding the section's opposed drink rooms.
The condemned circle between Hell and حَمِيمٍ آنٍ, using the same peak-heated sense as the section's spring already brought to its final boil.
The tree of Zaqqum is called the sinner's food, giving another concrete counterpart to the thorn food that cannot nourish.
That food boils inside bellies like molten metal, carrying kitchen language into punishment as the section does.
كَغَلْىِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ completes the cooking comparison with boiling water, joining food's ripeness to the infernal drink.
Garments of fire and boiling water poured over heads turn clothing and drink into the opposite of shelter and refreshment.
The poured water melts what is inside bellies and skins, completing the bodily effect introduced in 22:19.
In Hell they taste neither coolness nor drink, a direct deprivation opposite the garden's running spring and cups.
Only boiling water and foul fluid answer that deprivation, supplying the punitive drink itself.
The garden's inhabitants hear no لَغْوًا, only peace, while their provision comes morning and evening; hearing, empty speech, food, and the day's cycle meet.
عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مَّصْفُوفَةٍ combines the section's raised couches with its things arranged in rows in one garden furnishing.
A cup circulates in the garden with no لَغْوٌ and no sin around it, uniting the section's cups and absence of empty speech.
The companions are عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مَّوْضُونَةٍ, another direct formulation of the garden's prepared couches.
They recline facing one another on those couches, supplying the lived posture of the furnished room.
Cups, pitchers, and a goblet from a flowing spring reproduce the garden inventory of vessel and running source.
لَا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيهَا لَغْوًا repeats both the hearing and the excluded empty speech of 88:11.
Only repeated words of peace are heard there, stating what replaces the excluded لَغْو in 56:25.
وَفُرُشٍ مَّرْفُوعَةٍ brings spread bedding and elevation into one phrase, exactly meeting the section's raised furniture and spread carpets.
The garden dwellers recline on couches lined with brocade, another room whose unseen inner furnishing exceeds its visible surface.
They recline upon green cushions and fine carpets, directly repeating the section's paired cushion-and-carpet furnishings.
فِى جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ exactly repeats the high garden that receives the satisfied face.
The people of that high garden are told to eat and drink for what they sent ahead, joining provision to accepted labor.
Reclining on couches, the garden dwellers experience neither sun nor biting cold, making the room a perfected shelter.
Silver vessels and crystal cups circulate among them, repeating the placed cups of the section's garden.
عَلَى ٱلْأَرَائِكِ يَنظُرُونَ places looking upon garden couches, precisely joining the world's commanded gaze to the room it prefigures.
The radiance of bliss is recognized in their faces, completing the couch-and-gaze scene with the section's softened happy face.
عَلَى ٱلْأَرَائِكِ يَنظُرُونَ is repeated after the reversal of mockery, making the final gaze itself part of recompense.
The garden companions and spouses recline in shade upon couches, a compact parallel to the section's inhabited high room.
Golden trays and cups circulate while souls and eyes receive what delights them, joining vessel, desire, and sight in the garden.
وَكَأْسًا دِهَاقًا supplies the full cup within the same passage that excludes empty speech and calls the gift sufficient.
لَّا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيهَا لَغْوًا repeats the section's exact relation between garden hearing and worthless speech.
عَطَاءً حِسَابًا calls the garden reward an ample or sufficient gift, realizing the section's secondary sense of the حساب root inside a reckoning passage.
God does not take people to account for ٱللَّغْوِ in their oaths, supplying the section's bridge from speech excluded by hearing to what is excluded from reckoning.
لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِٱللَّغْوِ repeats the unaccounted oath sense and then distinguishes deliberate oaths that do count.
Everything people did is فِى ٱلزُّبُرِ; 54:53 then says every small and great thing is inscribed, joining labor to record.
The two receivers sit right and left to receive, locating the agents who keep the record that the Prophet does not control.
No spoken word is uttered without a watcher ready, bringing speech, hearing, and registration into a single act.
God hears secret and private speech while His messengers with them write it, another exact meeting of hearing and record.
Guardians are appointed over people, distinguishing the true overseers from the Messenger who is not مُصَيْطِر.
Those guardians are noble writers, identifying supervision specifically as inscription.
They know what people do, joining human labor to the divinely assigned record.
Every community is seen kneeling and summoned to its record, placing bodily lowering and accounting in the same Judgment scene.
God's book speaks truth because He had deeds copied, explaining who actually keeps the lines and count.
The laid-open record omits neither small nor great but enumerates it, while people find their deeds present before the just Lord.
God writes what people sent ahead and their traces and has enumerated everything in a clear register, joining labor, record, and divine count.
وَكُلَّ شَىْءٍ أَحْصَيْنَاهُ كِتَابًا makes comprehensive enumeration a book, the precise union of counting and lines.
God has counted the deeds people forgot and will report them at resurrection, separating human forgetfulness from divine accounting.
In the context of messengers delivering their Lord's messages, God encompasses what is with them and counts everything, placing conveyance and final oversight in their distinct roles.
After the just scales are set for Resurrection, وَكَفَىٰ بِنَا حَاسِبِينَ makes the حساب root mean both reckoning and divine sufficiency.
The person reads his own record and كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا joins sufficiency language directly to the Day's accounting.
وَكَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ حَسِيبًا fuses “sufficient” and “reckoner” in the compact wording behind the section's dictionary bridge.
Humanity labors painfully toward the Lord and will meet Him, joining exhausting work to the inevitable return.
Receiving the record in the right hand begins the favorable result of that labor.
فَسَوْفَ يُحَاسَبُ حِسَابًا يَسِيرًا promises an easy accounting, giving one end of the section's measure of sufficiency.
He returns joyfully to his people after the easy account, joining reckoning, happy face, and return.
The garden-bound person says he knew he would meet his حساب, placing confident anticipation immediately before the high garden.
The Prophet is not a compeller over them; فَذَكِّرْ بِٱلْقُرْءَانِ مَن يَخَافُ وَعِيدِ gives the same bounded reminder and fear-responsive audience as 88:21-22.
فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ repeats the command to remind while leaving reception outside the reminder's control.
سَيَذَّكَّرُ مَن يَخْشَىٰ identifies the one who fears as the hearer who accepts that reminder.
Insights have come from the Lord; whoever sees does so for himself, and the Prophet says he is not a guardian, joining sight to the limit on his role.
Whoever turns away from the Messenger is told that he was not sent as a keeper over them, matching turning away with the absence of control.
If they turn away, the Prophet was not sent as their guardian; his task is only conveyance, the same division of labor as reminder versus حساب.
The question whether the Prophet would compel people to become believers defines the same boundary expressed by لَّسْتَ عَلَيْهِم بِمُصَيْطِرٍ.
The Book is sent down in truth for people; guidance or loss returns to each person, while the Prophet is not their trustee.
فَٱتَّبِعْ سَبِيلَ مَنْ أَنَابَ إِلَىَّ invites the path of voluntary return, then إِلَىَّ مَرْجِعُكُمْ states the universal return that follows regardless.
وَأَنِيبُوا إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُمْ calls for willing return before punishment arrives, illuminating the section's difference between becoming an evvâb now and being returned later.
The garden is promised لِكُلِّ أَوَّابٍ حَفِيظٍ, naming the voluntary returner as the one welcomed into the favorable room.
The evvâb is one who feared the Merciful unseen and came with a penitent heart, connecting accepted reminder, fear, and willing inward return.
ٱرْجِعِى إِلَىٰ رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً مَّرْضِيَّةً is a welcomed and mutually pleasing return, the blessed opposite of the compulsory return of those who turn their backs.
إِنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ ٱلرُّجْعَىٰ states the same inescapable direction as 88:25 immediately after describing human transgression.
Everything in heaven and earth submits willingly or unwillingly and is returned to God, explicitly uniting the two modes of bending with the one final return.
All in heaven and earth prostrate willingly or unwillingly, as do their shadows morning and evening, joining voluntary and compelled lowering to the daily outward-and-homeward rhythm.
When told ٱرْكَعُوا they do not bow, giving the worldly refusal whose delayed bodily consequence appears in the humbled faces.
When the Quran is recited they do not prostrate, setting heard revelation and refused lowering against the posture of Judgment.
Humanity's حساب has drawn near while people remain heedless and turn away, bringing the final reckoning and the act of turning into one warning.
No renewed reminder comes from their Lord without their hearing it at play, sharpening the section's contrast between hearing the report and treating it as empty sound.
Dark pieces of night seem to have أُغْشِيَتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ, another Judgment image in which covering settles directly upon faces.
تَلْفَحُ وُجُوهَهُمُ ٱلنَّارُ makes the fire scorch faces, a direct parallel to the face-cooking water of 18:29.
Their faces are turned about in the Fire while they regret not obeying God and the Messenger, joining face, fire, and rejected message.
A person tries to shield himself with his face from the worst punishment, making the face the exposed boundary of the fire scene.
They are dragged on their faces into the Fire and told to taste its touch, combining the lowered face with burning punishment.
They emerge from graves with eyes lowered while تَرْهَقُهُمْ ذِلَّةٌ covers them, joining resurrection, gaze, and an enveloping abasement.
Some faces that Day are radiant, beginning the same division of eschatological faces as the section.
Other faces that Day have dust upon them, making the earth itself the visible ground of the abased face.
تَرْهَقُهَا قَتَرَةٌ says darkness covers those dusty faces, completing the section's cover-on-face image.
Some faces that Day are radiant, the positive face before the act of looking in 75:23.
إِلَىٰ رَبِّهَا نَاظِرَةٌ makes the blessed face a looking face, answering the section's earthly command to look.
Other faces that Day are gloomy, beginning the opposed half of the same facial diptych.
Those gloomy faces expect a crushing calamity, giving their expression its anticipated cause.
The Day when faces whiten and blacken supplies another explicit division of humanity by the state written on the face.
The whitened faces remain in God's mercy, completing the favorable side of the contrast begun in 3:106.
The condemned are shown to the Fire, humbled by abasement and looking with a furtive glance, joining fire, lowered stance, and diminished sight.
The nearer punishment is made to precede ٱلْعَذَابِ ٱلْأَكْبَرِ so that people may return, linking the section's greater punishment to the still-open chance of willing return.
The most wretched enters ٱلنَّارَ ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ, closely answering the section's heated fire and greater punishment.
He neither dies there nor lives, spelling out the impossible condition behind the drink from which death approaches on every side.
Only the most wretched enters the blazing fire, preparing the denial-and-turning explanation in the next ayah.
ٱلَّذِى كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ exactly joins denial and turning away as the path to that blaze.
وَٱلْأَرْضَ فَرَشْنَاهَا describes earth as something spread like bedding, making the world's floor the analogue of the garden's laid furnishings.
God makes earth بِسَاطًا, explicitly treating the terrestrial surface as a carpet.
That carpet enables travel through broad roads, giving the spread earth the daily journeying function evoked by the camel.
أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ ٱلْأَرْضَ مِهَادًا presents earth as a prepared bed, another direct construction of the world's furnished room.
The mountains are pegs, completing the tent-like earth image and matching the viewed mountains of 88:19.
God makes earth a settled place, heaven a structure, forms people well, and gives good provision, gathering room, creation, and sustenance.
Earth is made a cradle with paths, rain descends, and paired plants emerge, building the habitable landscape that feeds people and herds.
Earth is made a cradle and roads are placed in it so people may be guided, joining spread ground to purposeful travel.
The earth is extended, mountains set in it, and every balanced growth produced, a compact parallel to the section's spread earth and erected mountains.
وَكِتَابٍ مَّسْطُورٍ names an inscribed book with the same line-writing field the section associates with مُصَيْطِر.
وَٱلسَّقْفِ ٱلْمَرْفُوعِ turns the raised heaven into a lifted roof, directly supporting the section's world-as-room meeting.
The question أَمْ هُمُ ٱلْمُصَيْطِرُونَ uses the controlling sense of the same word, clarifying by contrast what the Prophet is denied in 88:22.
The heaven is built with power immediately before earth is spread in 51:48, supplying the roof above that furnished floor.
God gives earth life after its death and explains the signs so people may understand, making visible revival an intelligible proof.
Dead earth is a sign: God revives it and brings grain from it for people to eat, joining resurrection evidence directly to food.
God brings living from dead, dead from living, revives earth, and says وَكَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ, aligning natural revival with human emergence.
After the command to inspect food, poured water begins its making, the nourishing opposite of water poured or offered as punishment.
ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا opens the earth so food can grow, showing the prepared ground beneath the visual command.
Fruit and pasture stand among the foods produced, directly opposing the sterile thorn that neither fattens nor ends hunger.
مَّتَاعًا لَّكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ makes the food scene provision for people and their livestock, returning the gaze from food to the camel.
Immediately after the covering punishment of 12:107, the Prophet identifies his way as calling to God عَلَىٰ بَصِيرَةٍ, adding the messenger and lucid sight to that warning.
All return to God; He repeats creation to repay justly, while disbelievers receive boiling drink, joining return, recreation, accounting, and infernal water.
On the common camel reading of ٱلْجَمَلُ, those too proud for the signs cannot enter the garden until it passes through a needle's eye; the contemplated camel becomes the measure of excluded entry.
After the portable houses of 16:80, God gives shade, mountain shelters, and protective garments, extending the earthly shelter that anticipates the garden room.
أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱلْمَاءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ turns drinking water into an object of directed sight, joining the section's visual and drinking vocabularies.
The question whether people sent water from the cloud or God did locates the hidden giver behind the visible provision.
God could make that water bitter, marking the boundary between gracious drink and the punitive drink of boiling springs.
People are told to work; God, the Messenger, and believers will see the work, then all return to the Knower who reports it, joining labor, sight, message, and return.
A human being has only what he strove for, isolating the same سَعْي whose outcome divides the two groups of faces.
That striving will be seen, bringing labor itself under the gaze before recompense.
The striving is then repaid with the fullest repayment, completing the movement from work to account.
The coming Hour is kept hidden so every soul may be repaid for what it strives, joining concealed timing, effort, and the Day's measure.
Whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it faithfully has that striving appreciated, the accepted counterpart to the laboring face whose effort does not save it.
Garden dwellers are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they used to do, joining fulfilled labor with nourishing provision.
The righteous are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they used to do, another direct reversal of effort answered by food that cannot satisfy.
Hell becomes an inverted room: its bed is Jahannam and above it are غَوَاشٍ, coverings of fire; this immediately follows the camel-and-garden boundary in 7:40.
The fire's sparks appear like yellow camels, placing the animal contemplated as a created sign inside the punitive fire scene.
Hell throws sparks as large as a fortress, supplying the fiery object compared with camels in 77:33.
The condemned are ordered toward a three-branched shadow, beginning a shelter scene that reverses the garden room.
That shadow neither shades nor protects from flame, explicitly turning shelter into its opposite.
The companions of the left dwell amid scorching wind and boiling water, an infernal climate opposite the high garden's spring.
Their shade is black smoke, making the promised room itself a dark covering.
The smoky shade is neither cool nor pleasant, spelling out the failed shelter begun in 56:43.
The question أَفَلَا يُؤْمِنُونَ follows the joining and opening of heaven and earth and the making of every living thing from water, turning visible creation toward belief.
Firm mountains and broad paths are placed in earth after the water-and-creation sign, paralleling the section's viewed terrain.
Heaven is made a protected roof, a direct world-room counterpart to the raised garden furnishings, though people turn from its signs.
One ayah gathers heavens raised without visible pillars, mountains set in earth, scattered animals, rain, and noble growth—the full created landscape around the camel.
The oath by heaven and what built it repeats the section's question about how the sky was raised and made.
The paired oath by earth and what spread it repeats the downward movement from constructed heaven to prepared ground.
Water is driven to barren land, crops emerge for livestock and people to eat, and the ayah asks أَفَلَا يُبْصِرُونَ, joining dry earth, food, herd, and sight.
With eyes humbled, people emerge from graves like scattered locusts, directly joining lowered gaze to resurrection from the ground.
أَبْصَارُهَا خَاشِعَةٌ gives the trembling hearts of that Day the section's exact humbled-eye posture.
The Day of Resurrection displays those who lied about God with blackened faces, another judgment visibly written on faces.
When the promised event is seen near, the disbelievers' faces become distressed, joining sight, face, and the arrival they denied.
The condemned are gathered on their faces, blind, mute, and deaf, and their destination is Hell whose blaze is renewed.
Those gathered on their faces toward Hell are called worst in place and furthest from the way, making the lowered face the end of a misdirected journey.
When believers hear ٱللَّغْوَ they turn away from it, joining hearing, worthless speech, and a form of turning opposite to turning from the reminder.
Each person's deed is fastened to him and a record is brought out on Resurrection spread open; 17:14 then makes him read and reckon it.
Receiving the record in the right hand begins the sequence whose speaker joyfully says in 69:20 that he expected his account.
Receiving the record in the left hand begins the opposite account, matching the section's divided outcomes.
The condemned wishes he had never known what his حساب was, reversing the confident anticipation of 69:20.
Receiving the record behind one's back opens the adverse counterpart to the right-hand record of 84:7.
That person calls for destruction rather than returning joyfully, giving the emotional outcome of the adverse record.
He enters a blazing fire, completing the labor-to-record-to-fire sequence opposite 84:7-9.
The wicked person's record is in Sijjin, beginning the recorded opposite of the garden-facing couch scene later in the surah.
كِتَابٌ مَّرْقُومٌ specifies that adverse destiny as an inscribed record.
The righteous person's record is in Illiyyin, supplying the elevated recorded counterpart to Sijjin.
كِتَابٌ مَّرْقُومٌ repeats the inscribed-record formula for the righteous before their bliss and looking from couches.
When the scrolls are laid open, the act of spreading becomes the disclosure of recorded labor.
When Hell is set ablaze, the punitive room is made present in the same final unveiling as the opened records.
When the garden is brought near, the favorable room directly answers the blaze of 81:12.
Every soul then knows what it has brought, resolving record, fire, and garden into the result of its own work.
At Judgment the earth shines, the record is placed, messengers and witnesses are brought, and God judges truly, distinguishing delivery from judgment.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did, and God knows deeds best, completing the accounting scene.
The question whether the Prophet should identify the greatest losers in deeds directs attention to labor whose apparent exertion fails.
Their effort is lost in the nearer life while they think they are doing well, closely illuminating the section's laboring, exhausted face.
Because they deny the signs and meeting with their Lord, their deeds collapse and receive no weight on Resurrection.
إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ states that human striving diverges, supplying a compact key to the two opposite outcomes of effort in the section.
Giving and fearing God begin the path whose striving is eased toward ease.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ names the favorable destination of that striving.
Withholding and considering oneself self-sufficient begin the reversed path, pointedly misusing the notion of sufficiency.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ gives the adverse destination of the self-sufficient person's striving.
The one who wants only the immediate life receives a measured portion and then Hell, opposing the Hereafter-directed striving appreciated in 17:19.
Truth has come from the Lord; guidance benefits the hearer, straying harms him, and the Prophet is not a trustee over them.
Whenever a fresh reminder comes, people turn away from it, directly joining reminder and the section's act of turning.
They deny, so the reports of what they mocked will come to them, answering the opening question about whether the overwhelming report has arrived.
مُنِيبِينَ إِلَيْهِ is immediately joined to establishing prayer, bringing voluntary return and willing bodily worship together.
God creates all pairs and provides ships and livestock for people to ride, locating the mount within the created order.
Settling on the mounts' backs prompts remembrance of the One who subjected them, turning the journeying animal into recollection.
وَإِنَّا إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ makes every mounted journey rehearse the final return to the Lord.
Sacrificial camels are among God's signs; people are to mention God over them and then eat and feed others, joining camel, sign, and food.
وَلَا طَعَامٌ إِلَّا مِنْ غِسْلِينٍ exactly parallels the section's “no food except” construction with a second hell food.
Only sinners eat that food, locating the deprivation in the adverse account begun by the left-hand record.
Food that chokes and painful punishment give another concrete form of eating that cannot nourish or pass easily.
The ayah asks whether garden hospitality or the tree of Zaqqum is better, explicitly staging the two opposed provisions.
Zaqqum grows from the base of Hell, making the infernal food a grotesque reversal of growth from revived earth.
The condemned eat from it and fill their bellies, contributing the punitive meal itself.
A mixture of boiling water follows the food, repeating the section's food-and-scalding-drink sequence.
Their return is then to Hell, joining the meal to an adverse homecoming.
Water descends from heaven as drink and produces the vegetation in which livestock graze, joining drink, pasture, and herd.
The same water grows crops and fruits, extending the life-giving drink into human food.
Water enters earth, varied plants grow and then dry into debris, and the process is called a reminder, connecting viewed ground to impermanence and recollection.
The nearer life is likened to rain mingling with earth's food for people and livestock before the adorned ground is suddenly reaped bare.
Travel through earth should yield hearts that understand and ears that hear; the ayah says blindness belongs to hearts, joining landscape, walking, sight, and hearing.
Punishment covers the condemned from above and below while they are told to taste what they did, uniting enveloping punishment with recompensed labor.
Layers of fire above and below become the condemned person's shelter, the punitive inversion of roof, bedding, and room.
Those who fear their Lord receive lofty chambers built above chambers with rivers below, making elevation and constructed garden space explicit.
Believers who work righteousness are lodged in garden chambers beneath which rivers flow, joining accepted labor to the prepared room.
Resentment is removed and the garden dwellers sit as brothers on couches facing one another, completing the social room suggested by arranged furnishings.
No fatigue touches them and they are never expelled, reversing the exhausted labor and unstable nearer-world lodging.
The God-fearing are amid shade and springs, the real shelter and drink opposite the failed shade of 77:30-31.
They receive whatever fruit they desire, adding nourishing food to that shelter.
God says He thus rewards those who do good, identifying the room, drink, and food as the result of accepted work.
وَهَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ repeats the section's opening auditory question and begins a report that immediately turns to a seen fire.
Moses sees a fire during the journey and hopes to bring a brand or guidance from it, moving from received report to sight within the neighboring ayah.
The Arabic Quran is revealed so the Prophet may warn of the unquestioned Gathering Day, when one group is in the garden and another in the blaze.
The revelation is a reminder, and whoever wills may take a path to his Lord, expressing the voluntary response available before final return.
The passage is declared a reminder, defining the report's function rather than coercive control.
فَمَن شَاءَ ذَكَرَهُ leaves remembering to whoever wills, marking the hearer's voluntary response.
The question asks what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder, joining the Prophet's message to the section's turning away.
Their flight from the reminder is likened to startled wild donkeys, bringing a herd animal into the response-to-warning scene.
The herd flees a lion, completing the animal movement that images rejection of the reminder.
When the Fire sees them from far away, they hear its raging and roaring, bringing sight, hearing, and fire into one Judgment scene.
They are thrown bound into a narrow place within it, making punishment an oppressive room rather than an open, furnished one.
عَلَيْهِمْ نَارٌ مُّؤْصَدَةٌ makes fire close over them, another direct union of covering and flame.
إِنَّهَا عَلَيْهِم مُّؤْصَدَةٌ likewise describes the kindled fire as shut upon them, turning enclosure itself into punishment.
The inscribed book of 52:2 is فِى رَقٍّ مَّنشُورٍ, an opened or spread parchment that distinguishes the record's surface from what is written on it.
Food provisions, an added camel-load, and an easy measure occur together, an indirect meeting of camel, sustenance, and measured sufficiency.
The missing royal cup is linked to a promised camel-load of grain, bringing cup, camel, and measure together in a non-eschatological scene.
God creates every creature from water and gives different bodily forms of movement, a broader creation parallel that places the four-footed camel within water-made life.
Nearer life is rain-grown vegetation that delights observers and then withers into debris, while the Hereafter holds punishment or lasting forgiveness and pleasure.
The God-fearing occupy a secure station, the favorable dwelling opposite the preceding Zaqqum and boiling-water scene.
Gardens and springs furnish that secure station with the same paired setting as the section's high garden.
They wear fine silk and face one another, making the garden an inhabited room of ease after the infernal cooking imagery.
The purified servants sit on couches facing one another, the garden-room counterpart within the same passage that later describes Zaqqum.
A cup from a flowing spring circulates among them, pairing the furnished room with its drink.
The garden drink brings neither harm nor intoxication, a direct boundary against the scalding drink later in the passage.
Those deceived by nearer life receive boiling water and painful punishment for their disbelief, joining the punitive drink to failed response to reminder.
Those cast into Hell hear it roaring as it boils, giving the fire itself the overwhelming soundscape.
Its keepers ask each group whether no warner came, linking that heard fire to the rejected messenger who had only to warn.
